reader.title: Lynching of Howard Cooper
bases: Black and white papers alike say Cooper was 'lynched' at Towsontown, hanged from a sycamore tree, by what a Black correspondent called a mob (A2, A3, A5, A9).

Cooper was hanged from a sycamore at Towsontown without legal process, called a 'lynching' by the local paper and a 'lawless' slaying by a Black meeting (A2, A3, A5); the New York Freeman attributes it to 'the brainless mob at Towson' acting after an accusation that he assaulted a white girl (A9). The mob's size is not given.

The Baltimore County Union, the Towson Voice (via the Port Tobacco Times), the Cleveland Gazette's Hagerstown dispatch and the New York Freeman independently refer to Cooper's lynching at Towsontown (A3, A5, A8, A9), though no first report of the killing appears in the coverage.

summary.text: The lynching of Howard Cooper was the hanging of a Black man by a mob at Towsontown, Maryland, some time before July 25, 1885, after he was accused of assaulting a white girl.
He was hanged from a sycamore tree, which curiosity seekers later carried off in pieces.
The surviving coverage concerns the aftermath: Black protest and a false rumor that Black men would attack Towsontown in revenge.
No first report of the killing appears in the coverage; the earliest item, a Hagerstown dispatch dated July 25, 1885, already referred to "the Cooper hanging."

According to a Baltimore correspondent of the New York Freeman, Cooper had been accused of an assault on a white girl, and the city papers "immediately, in their editorials, set in judgment upon him."
Cooper was hanged from a sycamore tree in Towsontown by what the Freeman's correspondent called "the brainless mob at Towson."

A later Union item said that Keleher, jailed at Towsontown for a shooting, feared he might be "treated in the same manner that Cooper was," which suggests, without stating, that Cooper had been taken from that jail.
At Hagerstown about fifty Black residents met at Bethel A.M.E. Church and adopted resolutions against "the cruel and sudden slaying of any colored man accused of a revolting crime."
The resolutions called such killings "a stigma upon the fair name of Maryland" and urged Black Marylanders to assemble for their own protection.

In Baltimore a Black preacher named Gilmere delivered a sermon titled "Why Cooper was Lynched," but by mid-August the Freeman's correspondent complained that no indignation meeting had been held in the city.
Late in July a rumor spread that a body of Black men would come to Towsontown on the night of Friday, July 31, "in retaliation for the lynching of Cooper."
According to the Towson Voice, the rumor grew from two anonymous threatening letters to the sheriff and named the Black camp-meeting near town as the raiders' meeting place.
Some citizens met, a corporal's squad guarded the Towson Guards' armory that night, and Baltimore reporters drove out to find the town quiet.

The sheriff denied that he had expected an attack, and on Sunday the Rev. E. W. Scott, who led the camp-meeting, told his congregation that the reports were false, that he would help protect Sheriff Knight, and that "We have nothing to do with Howard Cooper's case."
Into late August curiosity seekers were carrying the tree away "piece-meal"; none of the items reports an inquest, an arrest or a trial.
The Baltimore County Union handled the lynching in short local items, among them a "conundrum" contrasting Zacheus, who "climbed a sycamore tree," with Cooper, who "was pulled up one."

Its editorials were aimed not at the killing but at the "worse than silly" retaliation rumor, which it called "a well-concocted lie," and at the Baltimore Morning Herald, whose reporter it named "the champion liar of the age."

The Towson Voice account, reprinted in the Port Tobacco Times under the headline "Simiar [Similar] to Martin Henry and Simpson Case," said the report was believed only by "a few of our most timid citizens."
The Black papers placed the killing in a pattern of lawlessness, the Cleveland Gazette running the Hagerstown resolutions under the headline "Condemning the Cooper Lynching."
The Freeman's correspondent set the editorials against Cooper beside the silence on assaults on Black women, citing a Hampstead case whose white accused "has not been arrested, much less lynched."

An earlier Freeman letter told the Herald, over its raid story, to "stop lying on colored people," so the Union and the Freeman both rejected the Herald's report, one as a hoax on the town, the other as a slander on Black people.

The Union described the rumored raiders as "a body of colored men" seeking retaliation for the lynching, and the Towson Voice as "a large number of colored people from Baltimore and Washington" bent on vengeance.
The Herald's version, as the Freeman described it, was instead a plan to lynch a white man jailed for mistreating a Black woman; the sheriff, according to the Voice, denied holding any such prisoner.

accounts.label: Local white weekly (Baltimore County Union)
accounts.gist: Refers to Cooper as 'lynched in Towsontown' on a sycamore, without describing the act; treats the later retaliation rumor as a hoax.

accounts.label: Towson Voice (reprinted)
accounts.gist: The rumored attack to avenge the lynching of Howard Cooper grew from anonymous letters to the sheriff and a warning to a Black woman; the sheriff denied the details.

accounts.label: Black correspondent, Baltimore
accounts.gist: Cooper was accused of assaulting a white girl and was killed by 'the brainless mob at Towson'; the press condemned him at once while ignoring assaults on Black women.

accounts.label: Hagerstown Black meeting
accounts.gist: Condemned 'the Cooper hanging' as part of a growing lawlessness in which accused Black men were slain without trial.

accounts.label: Baltimore Morning Herald (as described by others)
accounts.gist: Reported that Black people near Towsontown were raising a mob to break open the jail and lynch a white man held for mistreating a Black woman; both the Union and the Freeman called the report lies.

framing.detail: The Baltimore County Union printed a joke about Cooper being 'pulled up' a sycamore, called a Black minister's sermon on the lynching 'very absurd', and gave its editorial heat to the 'worse than silly' retaliation rumor rather than the killing.
The Towson Voice, reprinted under 'Simiar to Martin Henry and Simpson Case,' reported the rumor and the sheriff's denials as a 'foolish report' believed only by the timid.
The Cleveland Gazette headlined the Hagerstown resolutions 'Condemning the Cooper Lynching,' which called such slayings 'a stigma upon the fair name of Maryland.'
The New York Freeman's Baltimore letters called the lynchers 'the brainless mob at Towson,' the killing a 'barbarous act,' and the Herald's raid story lies about Black people.

conflicts.note: The Towson Voice says the sheriff denied that any white man charged with assaulting a Black woman was in his jail (A8); all three sources treat the rumor as false.
